extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and practitioners considering or defending inter partes reviews (IPRs)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to the IPR process before the PTAB, covering procedural requirements, substantive standards for invalidity challenges (anticipation/obviousness), strategic considerations for petitioners and patent owners, and appeal/settlement consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-or-nothing institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Supreme Court precedent and by rule, the PTAB must institute trial for all of the challenged claims or none of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects how petitioners draft petitions and how patent owners respond. Since SAS Institute, the PTAB often institutes on all claims while signaling some arguments are weak; inclusion of many weak grounds generally will not increase denial likelihood unless they drastically outnumber strong grounds. PTAB may sometimes institute when finding a 'reasonable likelihood' on a single claim or ground without analyzing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation (claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same legal standard for claim construction applies in an IPR and in a district court case: 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction positions taken during IPR proceedings may be used against a party in corresponding district court litigation; parties are encouraged to take consistent positions across proceedings. The PTAB will consider claim construction determinations and statements made in other proceedings and instructs parties to file relevant determinations as soon as available. Parties may propose constructions or state terms need no express construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stays of parallel litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a district court will stay litigation pending resolution of an IPR depends largely on whether the IPR has been instituted and how likely the IPR is to simplify the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider the stage of litigation, whether a stay will simplify issues, and potential prejudice to the patent owner. A petitioner should file any IPR petitions as early as possible after being sued to increase likelihood of a stay. For patent owners, defeating a petition at institution can avoid stay or prompt lifting of a pre-institution stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel after final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: After a final written decision, petitioners (and their privies and 'real parties-in-interest') are estopped from challenging a claim in court or before the USPTO on 'any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR proceeding (35 U.S.C. § 315(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has limited application in some contexts (e.g., may not apply to grounds on which PTAB declined to institute). Estoppel applies only to patent and printed publication prior art—not to product-based prior art developed before the date of invention—so petitioners may still challenge in court on product art. Questions persist about the meaning of 'reasonably could have raised.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend (claim amendments during IPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may file a motion to amend the patent after institution; the motion must clearly show changes and describe how disclosures in the original and priority applications support the proposed amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB rule changes (Mar 15, 2019) allow requesting preliminary guidance on the motion's merits and filing a revised motion. The petitioner ordinarily bears the burden to show by a preponderance of the evidence that proposed amended claims are unpatentable. Petitioners may submit new evidence in response and raise additional grounds (e.g., subject matter eligibility). Patent owners should carefully consider whether to request preliminary guidance because negative feedback may provide a roadmap for petitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and effect/timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties can settle an IPR proceeding but must file any settlement agreement with the PTAB and may do so under seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settling early is key because the PTAB may refuse to terminate a proceeding near completion and issue a final written decision. From a petitioner's perspective, settlement is advantageous because IPR estoppel does not apply to arguments raised in a settled proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for rehearing and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may seek rehearing at the PTAB (generally heard by the original panel) or appeal a final written decision to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearing deadlines: within 14 days of a non-final decision or a decision to institute; within 30 days of a final decision or a decision not to institute. Rehearing requests are unlikely to succeed. On appeal, the Federal Circuit reviews PTAB conclusions of law de novo and findings of fact for substantial evidence; IPR claim constructions generally reviewed de novo. Historically, the Federal Circuit has affirmed the PTAB about 75% of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and filing constraints (when an IPR is available)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR is available generally no earlier than 9 months after a patent's issue date; anyone other than the patent owner may petition; a petitioner who has been served with an infringement complaint must file within one year of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner must disclose real parties-in-interest. A petition cannot be filed if the petitioner has filed a declaratory judgment action challenging validity. Filing fee is at least $41,500. If petition is time-barred or other procedural defects exist, patent owner can raise those in preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal grounds and prior art considered
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR challenges are limited to anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) based on patents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation means a single reference discloses all claim elements; obviousness means one or more references in combination disclose or suggest claim elements such that a person of skill would have modified or combined teachings to arrive at the claimed invention. Product-based prior art is not part of IPR prior art scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and standard vs. federal court
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail, an IPR petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence—a lower burden than the clear and convincing standard in district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lower standard, combined with limited discovery and technically trained PTAB judges, generally makes challenging claims in IPRs easier and less costly than in federal court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery limits in IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules governing IPRs allow for limited discovery, including expert depositions and depositions of witnesses submitting declarations or affidavits, or discovery otherwise necessary in the interest of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery is much more constrained than in federal court; parties may move to seek additional limited discovery as part of post-institution briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition drafting requirements and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must submit a petition laying out specific grounds and supporting evidence; a petition must include and fully explain all arguments the petitioner wants to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner may only challenge based on patents and printed publications and may not expand arguments after filing except to respond to patent owner filings. Expert declarations should support arguments and explain how prior art discloses the invention without parroting attorney arguments or making conclusory statements. Generally file one petition; multiple parallel petitions are rare and require explanation and ranking to the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary response strategy for patent owners
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may file an optional preliminary response within three months of petition filing, but filing is not required and may be harmful if hastily prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preliminary response can preview arguments, address claim construction, and raise defenses such as time-bar, failure to list real parties-in-interest, unfairness due to prior IPRs, redundancy under § 325(d), or parallel litigation concerns (e.g., Fintiv). Patent owners must weigh the cost/time to prepare and whether to include an expert declaration, which may strengthen substantive arguments but can make success at institution less likely if it presents best arguments prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline, deadlines, and word limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Default IPR timeline is roughly 18 months from petition acceptance to final written decision (six-month petition phase and twelve-month trial phase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines: PTAB issues filing date notice a few weeks after petition; patent owner has up to 3 months for preliminary response; PTAB has 3 months to decide whether to institute after that; post-institution briefing schedule includes several 3-month and 6-week intervals; oral hearing occurs near the end; joinder can extend trial phase by ~6 months or more. USPTO limits petitions and responses to 14,000 words and replies/sur-replies to 5,600 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB institution decision finality
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB’s initial decision on whether to institute an IPR is 'final and nonappealable' (35 U.S.C. § 314(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because institution is final and nonappealable, the petition stage is critically important: a denied petition leaves the petitioner with no further recourse except rehearing, and an instituted review proceeds to final written decision unless settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder and effect on trial schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: If another petitioner moves to join an instituted IPR and the PTAB approves joinder, the trial phase may be extended (commonly six months or longer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder can change timing and procedural dynamics; petitioners filing parallel petitions must explain why multiple petitions should be instituted and rank them for PTAB consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing format and use of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The final written decision usually issues after an oral hearing where parties appear before a three-member PTAB panel for an hour or two to sum up arguments and answer questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR hearings typically rely on exhibits, testimony, and other evidence submitted before oral argument rather than live witnesses; parties may prepare demonstrative exhibits. A party can file a motion to request live testimony but PTAB rarely permits live testimony in practice.
